author: @capstacknick
caption:
$74M construction loan, closed this month. The Cove, Fort Lauderdale — 376 mixed-income units on a former hotel site. Developer: Affiliated Development. Lender: Pacific Life.

The detail worth noticing: the lender isn't a bank. It's a life insurance company. When bank construction lending tightens, insurance capital — long liabilities, patient money — steps into the gap. If you want to understand who actually funds development right now, watch who closes, not who advertises.

This is the tape. Real trades, real numbers, as they close — sometimes with my read on them.

Comment CAPSTACK and I'll DM you the map of who's who in a deal — and which seat you can actually take.

author: @capstacknick
caption:
Multifamily development right now: high-teens IRRs, 1.6–2x multiples.

Here’s the problem. Investors can get those same numbers buying EXISTING buildings, because prices have come down. Same return, none of the construction risk.

So why would their capital fund your ground-up deal?

That question should pick your asset class — not what you love, not what the podcasts are pushing. Capital flows to the best risk-adjusted return, and it does not care about your preferences.

Before you commit to a lane, find out what the check writers in your market are actually funding. Match yourself to the money. Don’t ask the money to match you.

author: @capstacknick
caption:
I spent years chasing deals. Now they come to me - about $800M of deal
flow, inbound.

A sponsor sent me a deal in my DMs. Another came through a connection
who knew exactly what I do. I found neither one.

The most valuable asset in development isn’t capital. It’s being the
person deals come to. Everyone competes for the deals that get
marketed. Almost nobody sees the ones that don’t.

The mechanism: real knowledge builds credibility, credibility brings
inbound, inbound becomes partnerships. Pick a lane narrow enough to
actually know - one asset type, three markets. Breadth reads as a
beginner.

And to be straight with you: this account is that funnel. You’re
watching it run in real time.

author: @capstacknick
caption:
Every real estate deal has two owners. Everybody wants to be the first
one. The second one is the seat you can actually take.

Owner #1 is the lead sponsor. They found the site, they wrote the
business plan, they carry the risk. That's the job everyone pictures —
and almost nobody gets it on their first deal.

Owner #2 is the partner who fills the gap. Because almost no lead
sponsor has everything a deal needs. They need someone to raise the
equity, someone whose balance sheet can sign the loan and completion
guarantees, and someone who can actually execute the plan. Most
sponsors are short at least one of the three.

Fill one of those gaps and you're the co-GP. Not an investor. Not an
employee. A partner — on a deal you put no money into. And you get paid
like one: above what the investors are owed, the sponsors split an extra
share of the profit. That's the promote. Fill a gap, you share in it.

Stop trying to be Owner #1 on day one. Be the person Owner #1 can't
finish without.

Comment GAP and I'll DM you the one-page map of who's who in a deal —
every seat at the table, in plain English, including the one you can
actually take.

author: @capstacknick
caption:
Repositioning a hotel for Steve Witkoff taught me something no spreadsheet
ever could: your renovation budget is a guess until you open the walls.

We opened the walls expecting a normal reno. Instead: concrete that was
basically beach sand — old South Florida construction, the mix had been
cut decades earlier. A multi-million-dollar surprise, and none of it was
in the pro forma.

The fix isn't being smarter. It's carrying real contingency. Ground-up
build: ~5%. Renovation or adaptive reuse: 10-15%+, because you can't
price what you can't see. If your reno budget has a 5% contingency, you
don't have a budget — you have a hope.

Save this before your next underwrite.

author: @capstacknick
caption:
"I don't have the money to get into real estate development." It's the thing I hear most from people who want to break into institutional real estate — and it's not the real barrier.

My first development deal: a Boston sponsor had the site but a gap — capital relationships and underwriting. I couldn't write the equity check. I could build the model, and I had the Rolodex. So I rolled my fee in as equity instead of taking cash, and earned a co-GP slice of a $73M deal.

Swipe for the exact structure. Save it for the day you need it.
